title: Should I not have pity? (Jonah 4)
hookLine: God asks Jonah: should I not pity Nineveh, and much cattle too?
carry: doest thou well to be angry

cards: Jonah finally goes to Nineveh and cries out that the great city will be overthrown. And it works. The people believe.
They fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king comes down from his throne and sits in ashes. God sees them turn from their evil way, and doesn't bring the disaster.
A whole city spared. A prophet might be expected to rejoice. In the King James words: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry."

teach.b: Now we learn why he ran. Jonah tells God, in the King James words: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil."
He quotes God's mercy back at God, as a complaint: he knew the city would be forgiven, and didn't want it. God answers with a question: doest thou well to be angry? Jonah doesn't answer.
He goes out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to watch. God makes a plant grow over him for shade, a kikayon, a gourd in the King James, and Jonah is exceedingly glad of it.
Next dawn, a worm attacks it and it withers. A hot east wind blows, the sun beats on his head, and Jonah says he'd rather die.

teach.h: A GOURD THAT GREW AND WITHERED.
teach.b: Then God speaks the book's last words: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night:" And: "And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?"

teach.h: SHOULD NOT I HAVE PITY ON NINEVEH?
teach.b: The 1917 Jewish translation has: should not I have pity. And the book stops. We never hear Jonah's answer; the question is left for whoever reads it next.
Even the animals are in it: God's pity reaches the cattle of a foreign city.

teach.h: THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.
teach.b: On Yom Kippur afternoon, Jews read this whole book, and it ends right here.

how: Jews read the whole book of Jonah at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur, ending with God's question about pity for Nineveh.

games.q: you're Jonah. the city you warned has turned and been spared. God asks, doest thou well to be angry? what do you do?
o: go out and sit east of the city, watching.
games.why: Jonah doesn't answer. he sits outside the city to watch, and God teaches him with a gourd.

practice: Let your circle of good wishes go one step out, toward someone from a place or group you'd rather not see spared, a city in the news, a rival team, the far side of an argument, though not someone who wronged you.
You don't have to agree with them; just let God's question to Jonah be asked about them: should there be no pity here? If you pray, you can pray for their good.

wordCard.voice: kikayon, the plant God grew to shade Jonah, then let a worm destroy, the gourd of the King James. Today's word.
